cons: Every yuan must be traced to documented, taxed income; untaxed income must be taxed first; done at the branch with originals.
limit: No fixed quota: the amount is whatever the income and tax documents support. The USD 50,000 annual total applies to domestic individuals, not to this route.
name: Documented China income → bank conversion
pros: The standard route written into the rules; any amount the documents support; the bank reviews where the RMB came from, not what you will do with the dollars.
who: A foreign passport holder whose RMB is lawful China-source current-account income (salary, service fees and similar) with tax records.

cons: Useless once the memo is older than 24 months or lost; covers only the unused part.
limit: Up to the unused amount on the memo; the memo is valid for 24 months from the exchange date. Without a memo: up to USD 500 equivalent a day with ID only.
name: Convert back RMB you originally exchanged from foreign currency
pros: No income or tax papers needed — the memo is the proof.
who: Anyone holding RMB that came from their own earlier foreign-currency exchange and still holding the original exchange memo.

cons: Does not apply to a balance already held in RMB.
limit: The unused foreign-currency balance; returned the way it came.
name: Send back foreign currency that was wired in and never converted
pros: No conversion at all, so no exchange margin; ID only.
who: Holders of a foreign-currency balance in China that arrived from abroad and was not converted to RMB.

cons: Needs the registered transfer and tax documents; income tax of 20% applies to the gain on the sale itself.
limit: Sale price minus the taxes of that sale.
name: Proceeds of selling your home in China
pros: Handled by the bank; large amounts possible in one go.
who: An overseas individual who sold a home held in their own name, after the ownership transfer is registered.

cons: Approval by the SAFE branch where the deceased was registered; proof of inheritance, property and tax documents; no cash withdrawal.
limit: The approved amount; one or several remittances.
name: Inherited estate in China (foreign-citizen heir)
pros: A defined approval route for large sums; paid straight to your own account abroad.
who: A foreign citizen who lawfully inherited property in China and has turned it into cash.

cons: Needs proof that household registration was cancelled and of settlement abroad certified by a Chinese consulate, plus tax certificates; SAFE approval. Not available to someone who was never a mainland resident.
limit: The approved amount; since 2014 one or several remittances (no forced staging).
name: Emigrant property transfer
pros: Covers whole pre-emigration wealth, not only income.
who: Only someone who moved from mainland China and settled abroad, for lawful property owned before obtaining emigrant status.

cons: Requires a real company and completed liquidation or a real profit distribution; tax filing above USD 50,000. The profit-remittance procedure itself was not re-read.
limit: Distributed profit, or the investor's share after liquidation and tax.
name: Profit or liquidation proceeds of your China company
pros: Liquidation proceeds are explicitly allowed by the State Council Regulation after tax.
who: A foreign investor in a registered foreign-invested enterprise.

cons: Banks along the route may deduct an unpublished amount.
name: Bank of China wire, standard
pros: Lowest verified all-in cost; fee capped at CNY 260 + 150.
who: Any customer whose conversion is approved under one of the entitlements above.

cons: USD 25 extra (USD 15 if the receiving bank holds an account with BOC New York).
limit: USD wires; see note 5 of the tariff for scope.
name: Bank of China wire, full-amount arrival
pros: No deduction by intermediary banks.
who: As above, when the receiving bank must get the exact amount.

cons: Standard cap CNY 500 + 120 is higher than BOC; exchange margin not verified.
name: HSBC China wire
pros: Fee waived for private-banking individual customers.
who: HSBC China Premier or Advance customers; free for private-banking individual customers.

cons: The only official page found is dated 2016; exchange margin not verified.
name: China Construction Bank wire
pros: Low minimum fee on the page found.

cons: No current official tariff could be opened — nothing is priced.
name: ICBC and other Chinese banks

cons: Only salary-type money with tax records; many transfers for large sums; fee not published on the help page.
limit: CNY 300,000 per transfer from a China bank app (CNY 50,000 from Alipay); overall limit about your after-tax China salary.
name: Wise, sending from CNY
pros: Fully online; no branch visit.
who: Not mainland Chinese; working or worked in China; Chinese tax record with tax paid in the last 3 years; recipient is your own account.

cons: About USD 15,000 a year at most; issuer fee about 1.1% plus unknown network rate and ATM surcharge; going over the cap suspends the card abroad for two years.
limit: CNY 100,000 per person per calendar year; CNY 10,000 per card per day.
name: Cash withdrawals abroad with a mainland bank card
pros: No documents; works for small sums.
who: Any holder of a mainland bank card.

cons: Does not avoid the conversion documents; dozens of crossings for large sums; theft risk; above USD 10,000 must be reported to US customs.
limit: USD 5,000 per crossing without a permit; USD 5,000–10,000 with a bank-issued permit; above USD 10,000 not allowed in principle.
name: Carry US-dollar cash out of China
pros: No wire fee.
who: A traveller who has first lawfully bought and withdrawn the dollars.

cons: Pays for purchases only — it does not put dollars in your US account. Rules and fees for card spending were not verified.
limit: Not verified. The SAFE cap read here covers cash withdrawals.
name: Spend abroad on a mainland card instead of converting
who: Any holder of a mainland bank card.

cons: No official rule or tariff for individuals was opened in this session — nothing is asserted.
name: Remit the RMB abroad and convert offshore

cons: Private or disguised buying and selling of foreign exchange: fine up to 30% of the amount, 30%–100% if serious, illegal gains confiscated; operators commit the crime of illegal business operations; funds can be frozen or lost.
name: Underground banks and private currency swaps
pros: None that survives the risk.

cons: Splitting to evade limits is expressly forbidden; treated as evasion or fraudulent purchase of foreign exchange: fine up to 30%, 30%–100% if serious.
name: Splitting through other people's USD 50,000 quotas
pros: None.

cons: Obtaining foreign exchange with false or invalid documents: funds converted back, fine up to 30%, 30%–100% if serious, criminal liability.
name: False invoices, contracts or invented transactions
pros: None.

cons: Exchanging legal tender and virtual currency in the mainland is an illegal financial activity, strictly prohibited; no legal protection if the counterparty disappears.
name: Crypto or stablecoin conversion
pros: None.

cons: Expressly prohibited; overseas withdrawals suspended for the current and next year once the cap is exceeded.
name: Borrowed or lent bank cards for overseas cash
pros: None.

cons: China: warning and fine up to 20% of the amount. United States: more than USD 10,000 must be reported on FinCEN Form 105; family members may not split amounts.
name: Undeclared cash above the limits
pros: None.
